> Nandakumar M, Lundberg M, Carlsson F, Råberg L (2025). Positive Selection on Mammalian Immune
> Genes: Effects of Gene Function and Selective Constraint. *Molecular Biology and Evolution*
> 42(1):msaf016. <https://doi.org/10.1093/molbev/msaf016>. Open access under CC BY.
> Code: <https://github.com/lraberg/PositiveSelectionRodentImmuneGenes>

| Field | |
|---|---|
| **Year** | Published 21 January 2025 |
| **Models** | **30 rodent genomes**: 15 Muridae and 15 Cricetidae, house mouse as reference. Population data from wild house mouse and bank vole |
| **Brain region** | **None.** Immune genes across the whole body. Expression taken from ten organs as a covariate |
| **Measures** | **DNA.** Coding sequence between species, plus polymorphism within species |
| **Method** | Orthologues from TOGA annotations, PRANK codon alignments, IQ-TREE2 gene trees. 977 immune genes and 1,005 control genes after filtering |
| **Cross-species stats** | **BUSTED** (HyPhy), gene-wide on the full CDS, model-averaged over three variants, Benjamini-Hochberg correction. CODEML M1a vs M2a for comparison. **dN/dS** and **pN/pS** compared between categories with Dunnett's tests |

: {tbl-colwidths="[22,78]"}

## My reading

I looked at the paper called Positive Selection on Mammalian Immune Genes: Effects of Gene
Function and Selective Constraint. What the researchers did, they wanted to look at the
**immune genes that are targets for positive selection**. Positive selection is a process in
which genes are favoured and reproduced if their function ensures a higher likelihood of
survival.

They took **rodents** to analyse the mammalian immune genes. They looked at **gene function,
gene expression, protein-protein interaction**, and also the **selective constraint**. They
looked at **pattern recognition receptors, PRRs**, which were expected to have a higher
positive selection rate than other genes. They also expected that for **cytokines** and for
**cell surface proteins**. And they reasoned that the gene function might determine the
positive selection.

I noted down that they worked a lot with selective constraint, **pN divided by pS**, and also
**dN divided by dS**, which we also used when we looked at the CDS.

So the focus is essentially that they wanted to see **what immune genes were key targets for
positive selection**, and whether the enrichment of signatures of positive selection in certain
genes is a **direct effect of gene function or an indirect effect of other factors**.

They looked at the **Cricetidae and Muridae** families, and they found that there were around
**1,100 genes** that they could divide into **six categories**, which proved their initial
assumptions. The genes that they used were screened against other sources to check whether the
immune function was covered by **at least two sources**. They also needed this categorization to
separate the **host pathogen genes** from the other ones, because the host pathogen genes have a
**co-evolution** process which the other genes might not have, and this might also influence
the positive selection.

They also had **control genes**. I am not quite sure why this approach works, in which they just
took randomly **1,300 protein-coding mouse genes** which are not associated with immune related
processes. So I am thinking that when they take random genes, which should not express a high
positive selection because they are not related to the immune system in any way, they can use
this as a **baseline** for their genes that do show a higher positive selection. I think.

They tested for positive selection with **dN/dS**. They looked at the CDS for the dN/dS, but
they noticed that the CDS rarely allows for a positive selection calculation, so they used
**BUSTED**. I will say I skipped this because I did not think it was very important for me.

What they saw is that immune genes had signatures of positive selection, including **Tlr1 and
Ifih1**, and there were also some in the cytokines. Then they compared the full protein CDS
with **Dunnett's test**, to check, I believe, for a correlation. They saw that there is a
**higher positive selection in cytokines and cell surface proteins**, and the differences in
pN/pS match the different categories they assigned the immune genes to based on their gene
function.

In the discussion they note that **PRRs, cytokines and cell surface proteins had similar,
higher proportions** of genes with signatures of positive selection than control genes. But for
the PRR genes, since there are not that many in the genome that they could use in a
bioinformatical way, they state that there is **limited statistical power**, so it cannot be
completely generalized. It does give you a hint that there might be a higher positive
selection. They also note the co-evolution of host and pathogen, which I also kind of skipped.
And they discuss why **cytokines and cell surface proteins are common targets of pathogen immune
evasion**, and how that raises the proportion of positive selection in those genes.

## What I take from it

They worked a lot with pN/pS and dN/dS, which we also used when we looked at the CDS. And the
random control genes, which are not related to the immune system in any way, work as a
baseline for the genes that do show a higher positive selection.

## Checks against the paper

- **Immune cells or immune genes?** Genes. The title is Positive Selection on Mammalian Immune
  *Genes*.
- **Around 1,100 genes in six categories?** 1,273 immune genes were collected, 1,112 fit one of
  the six categories, and 977 passed alignment filters. The six are PRRs, cytokines, other cell
  surface proteins, intracellular signalling, extracellular proteases, and effectors.
- **Covered by at least two sources?** Yes, at least two of four: Amigo2, KEGG, PANTHER and
  Reactome.
- **Why do random control genes work?** As you thought, they are the background rate. Controls
  are not free of positive selection, 8.9% of them showed it against 13.0% of immune genes. The
  question is whether immune genes sit above that.
- **The CDS rarely allows a positive selection calculation?** BUSTED still runs on the full
  CDS. It asks whether some sites on some branches have dN/dS above 1, which an average over the
  whole gene rarely shows.
- **Dunnett's test for a correlation?** Not a correlation. It compares each category against
  the control group.
- **Higher selection in cytokines and cell surface proteins?** Yes. But once pN/pS was
  accounted for, only cytokines stayed higher than controls. The authors read cytokines as a
  direct effect of function, and cell surface proteins as mostly an indirect effect of low
  constraint.
- **Expression and protein-protein interaction?** Neither predicted positive selection once the
  category was taken into account.
- **Limited power for PRRs?** Yes. 3 of 56 PRRs were under positive selection, so the difference
  from controls was not significant.

## Open questions from this read

- How does BUSTED work, and why is it preferred over CODEML here? Skipped on this read.
- The host pathogen co-evolution part of the discussion. Skipped on this read.

## How it relates to this project

1. **It uses the same measure.** dN/dS on aligned coding sequence is what this project uses for
   conservation, so it is a worked example of that measure on a published gene set.

2. **It uses a control set the same way.** Random genes outside the category of interest as a
   baseline is the comparison this project makes between BBB genes and its control genes.

3. **It names an established algorithm.** BUSTED is a candidate for a positive selection test in
   the method-driven pipeline, next to the dN/dS ratio itself.

## Reference detail from the paper

- **Proportion under positive selection** (BUSTED model-average): 89 of 1,005 control genes
  (8.9%) against 127 of 977 immune genes (13.0%), P = 0.0030. At FDR q < 0.2: 20 (2%) against
  37 (3.8%).
- **By category:** cytokines and cell surface proteins higher than controls (Dunnett's P = 0.014
  and 0.023). Effectors and proteases each under 50 genes, with only one or two selected.
- **dN/dS:** every immune category except intracellular signalling higher than controls;
  signalling lower (P = 0.0005).
- **pN/pS:** mean of house mouse (Harr et al. 2016, German samples, N = 8) and bank vole
  (Lundberg et al. 2020, N = 31). PRRs, cytokines and cell surface proteins higher than
  controls (P ≤ 0.013); signalling lower (P = 0.0029).
- **Named genes under positive selection:** Ifih1 and Tlr1 (PRRs), Ifnb1 and Il12b (cytokines),
  Ifngr2 and Il12rb1 (cytokine receptors), Cd80 (cell surface). Full list in supplementary
  table S2.
